parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the centre of gravity of an object.

markscheme_points.text: point where (all) the weight (of an object) is taken to act

hints: Hint 1: Think about how you can replace the weight of every tiny part of an extended object by one single force acting at one special point when doing moments or balance.
parts.proper_answer: The point at which all the weight of the object is taken to act.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What centre of gravity means**
Imagine an object is made of lots of tiny pieces, each with its own tiny weight pulling down. For balance and turning effects you do not need to track them all separately. You can pretend the total weight pulls down from just one point. That point is the centre of gravity.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A uniform beam $AB$ is attached by a frictionless hinge to a vertical wall at end $A$. The beam is held so that it is horizontal by a metal wire $CD$, as shown in Fig. 3.1.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1 (not to scale)

The beam is of length $0.96\text{ m}$ and weight $23\text{ N}$. A block of weight $W$ rests on the beam at a distance of $0.20\text{ m}$ from end $B$. The wire is attached to the beam at point $D$ which is a distance of $0.40\text{ m}$ from end $B$. The wire exerts a force on the beam of $45\text{ N}$ at an angle of $37^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The beam is in equilibrium.
parts.text: Calculate the vertical component of the force exerted by the wire on the beam.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the 45 N arrow making 37 degrees with the horizontal and picture its force triangle - which side of the triangle is vertical and opposite the 37 degree angle?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Splitting the angled pull into up and across**
The wire pulls at 37 degrees above the beam, so part of the pull lifts up and part pulls sideways. The vertical part is the side opposite 37 degrees in the right-angled force triangle.

Step 2: **Calculate the vertical lift**
$$F_{v} = 45 \sin 37^{\circ}$$ $$F_{v} = 27\text{ N}$$ This acts upward on the beam at D.

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the 45 N arrow making 37 degrees with the horizontal and picture its force triangle - which side of the triangle is vertical and opposite the 37 degree angle?
walkthrough:

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: By taking moments about $A$, calculate the weight $W$ of the block.

markscheme_points.text: the magnitudes of the three moments about A are (23 × 0.48), (27 × 0.56) and (W × 0.76) correct magnitude of any one moment about A
correct magnitudes of any two moments about A

hints: Hint 1: Think about taking all turning effects about the hinge A so the unknown hinge force drops out, and list which forces try to turn the beam clockwise and which try to turn it anticlockwise.
Hint 2: Work out the perpendicular distance from A for each force: the beam weight acts at its midpoint, the vertical wire component acts at D, and W acts beyond D.
Hint 3: Set total clockwise moment equal to total anticlockwise moment about A and rearrange to find W.
parts.proper_answer: Taking moments about A: $(23 \times 0.48) + (W \times 0.76) = 27 \times 0.56$, giving $W = 5.4\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why moments about A is clever**
You have hinge forces at A that you do not know. Moment is force times perpendicular distance from the pivot. Any force through A has zero moment about A, so it disappears from the equation. That leaves only three moments.

Step 2: **Find each distance from A**
The beam is uniform, length $0.96\text{ m}$, so its $23\text{ N}$ weight acts at the middle: $$0.96 / 2 = 0.48\text{ m from A}$$ Point D is $0.56\text{ m}$ from A. The block is $0.20\text{ m}$ beyond D, so: $$0.56 + 0.20 = 0.76\text{ m from A}$$

Step 3: **Balance clockwise against anticlockwise**
The $23\text{ N}$ and $W$ pull down, giving clockwise moments. The $27\text{ N}$ vertical component from (b)(i) pulls up at D, giving an anticlockwise moment. For equilibrium: $$\text{sum of clockwise moments} = \text{sum of anticlockwise moments}$$ $$(23 \times 0.48) + (W \times 0.76) = 27 \times 0.56$$ $$11.04 + 0.76W = 15.12$$ $$0.76W = 4.08$$ $$W = 5.4\text{ N}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The hinge exerts a force on the beam at end $A$.

Calculate the horizontal component of this force.
hints: Hint 1: Look again at the same 45 N triangle but this time focus on the side along the beam next to the 37 degree angle, and remember the beam has no other horizontal push except from the hinge.
parts.proper_answer: $45 \cos 37^{\circ} = 36\text{ N}$, so hinge provides $36\text{ N}$ in the opposite direction.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balancing the sideways pull**
The wire also drags the beam toward the wall. The beam stays still, so the hinge must push back equally and oppositely to keep horizontal forces balanced.

Step 2: **Calculate the sideways part**
The horizontal part is adjacent to the 37 degree angle: $$F_{h} = 45 \cos 37^{\circ} = 36\text{ N}$$ So the hinge exerts a $36\text{ N}$ horizontal force on the beam.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text:
The block is now placed closer to point $D$ on the beam.

State whether this change will increase, decrease or have no effect on the tension in the wire.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the clockwise moment of W about A when its distance from A gets smaller, and what that means for the anticlockwise moment the wire must supply.
parts.proper_answer: Decrease. The moment of W about A is reduced, so a smaller moment and hence smaller tension is needed from the wire to maintain equilibrium.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Smaller distance means smaller turning effect**
Moment is force times distance. Moving the same weight W closer to A and to D shortens its distance, so its clockwise moment about A gets smaller. The beam weight moment is unchanged. To keep balanced, the anticlockwise moment from the wire must also get smaller, so the tension in the wire decreases.

parts.label: (b)(v)
parts.text:
The stress in the wire is $5.3 \times 10^{7}\text{ Pa}$. The wire is now replaced by a second wire that has a radius which is three times greater than that of the original wire. The tension in the wire is unchanged.

Calculate the stress in the second wire.

markscheme_points.text: σ = F / πr² or 4F / πd² so σ = 5.3 × 10⁷ × πr² / π(3r)² = 5.3 × 10⁷ / 9 = 5.9 × 10⁶ Pa

hints: Hint 1: Recall how stress links tension force to the cross-sectional area of the wire, and think about how area depends on radius.
Hint 2: If radius becomes $3r$, area becomes $9$ times larger, so for the same force work out what happens to stress by dividing by $9$.
parts.proper_answer: $\sigma = F/A$ with $A = \pi r^{2}$. New area is $9$ times larger, so $\sigma = 5.3 \times 10^{7} / 9 = 5.9 \times 10^{6}\text{ Pa}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stress spreads force over area**
Stress tells you how concentrated the pull is: $$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$$ where $A = \pi r^{2}$ for a circular wire.

Step 2: **Scale the area then the stress**
Tension $F$ is unchanged. New radius $= 3r$, so: $$A_{new} = \pi (3r)^{2} = 9\pi r^{2} = 9A_{old}$$ Stress is inversely proportional to area, so it falls by a factor of $9$: $$\sigma_{new} = \frac{5.3 \times 10^{7}}{9} = 5.9 \times 10^{6}\text{ Pa}$$
